before.label: Michel Foucault
before.description: Investigates historical conditions of knowledge, power, and subject formation. Archaeology and genealogy provide related but changing approaches.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Order of Things (1966); Discipline and Punish (1975); History of Sexuality I (1976). His association with structuralism is contested.

after.label: Michel Foucault
after.description: Studies how objects of knowledge and subjects take shape through historically specific practices. Archaeology examines discursive formations; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Power works through actions upon possible actions, with institutions, resistance and changing forms of subjectivity entering the analysis.
after.representative_figures_and_works: The Order of Things (1966); Discipline and Punish (1975); History of Sexuality I (1976). His association with structuralism is contested.
after.scope_note: Individual thinker with changing projects, not a uniform structuralist school. History of Madness (1961), archaeological inquiry, genealogy and the 1982 account of subjects are distinct contexts. Canguilhem and Nietzsche supply named resources. Derrida’s challenge and Foucault’s reply concern reason, madness, Descartes and discursive practice; neither settles their whole relationship. Historians including Scott, Chartier, Goldstein, Said and Stoler adapt and criticize different aspects, with separately scoped evidence. Comparative historical generalizations remain attributed. Later ethics and self-practice require further bounded primary reading.

before.label: Jacques Derrida
before.description: Examines instabilities and exclusions in conceptual oppositions and accounts of meaning. Engages structuralism critically rather than simply extending it.
before.representative_figures_and_works: “Structure, Sign, and Play” (1966); Of Grammatology (1967). Husserl and Heidegger are further important interlocutors beyond the links selected here.

after.label: Jacques Derrida
after.description: Works through conceptual hierarchies and the conditions of signification, writing and historical transmission. Critical engagements with Saussure, Husserl, Heidegger and Foucault distinguish deconstruction from a single structuralist method. His archive inquiry connects institutions, access, inscription and preservation with psychoanalytic questions.
after.representative_figures_and_works: “Structure, Sign, and Play” (1966); Of Grammatology (1967). Husserl and Heidegger are further important interlocutors beyond the links selected here.
after.scope_note: Individual thinker whose arguments change across works. Of Grammatology (French 1967; first American 1976; corrected English 1997) is distinct from the 1963 Cogito lecture, 1983 Japanese letter and 1994 archive lecture. Peirce, Freud and historian Sonia Combe are explicit resources in the selected passages. Scott and Spivak offer particular productive uses; Foucault supplies a specific objection. Deconstruction is not a license for arbitrary readings or a claim that institutions reduce to books. The original French witnesses, full archive argument and Austin/Searle exchange remain outside this bounded primary reading.
